title: An Interaction Is All You Need — Ivan Leo, Google DeepMind
description:
Models became agents, and the APIs didn't keep up. Google DeepMind rebuilt them.

Ivan Leo, developer experience engineer at Google DeepMind, introduces the Gemini Interactions API and Managed Agents. He traces how we went from single completions to function calling to agents, then shows server-side state with interaction IDs (no more hand-managing thought signatures), strongly typed multimodal outputs, mixing built-in and custom tools, and the new steps data model. He then demos Managed Agents, which run the Antigravity harness in a persistent remote sandbox with environment IDs, loadable sources, a credential-injecting proxy and named agents, plus the open-source Gemini API CLI.

In this talk:
• Why agent workloads need a different API shape
• Server-side state: interaction IDs and thought signatures
• Chaining image, video and audio generation with the same context
• Managed Agents: persistent sandboxes, skills, secure credentials and named agents

title: I Built a Personal AI Agent on a Raspberry Pi — Jeremy Adams, Neo4j
description:
No Mac Mini, no laptop agent. Jeremy Adams runs his personal AI agent on an old Raspberry Pi he wears around his neck.

Jeremy Adams, senior developer advocate at Neo4j, assembles a wearable AI agent live on stage: NanoClaw on a Raspberry Pi 4B, messaged over WhatsApp, with Docker-isolated agents and a Neo4j graph database. He shows how he built graph memory using the POLE schema (person, object, location, event) mid-flight, added voice-to-text through a USB mic and a hardware button, ran an offline mode with a local Neo4j, and walked the AI Engineer expo floor turning booth notes into a graph of themes. He finishes by upgrading to Neo4j Agent Memory.

In this talk:
• Why a small, hackable claw beats a feature-rich agent on your laptop
• Connecting an agent to Neo4j over MCP
• Graph memory with the POLE schema
• Offline-first capture with a local graph that syncs and enriches in the cloud

title: AI Safety Expert WARNS: We're NOT Ready For They're Preparing
description:

Nate Soares warns that the most likely outcome of increasingly autonomous AI may be systems acting on their own initiative, after AI agents demonstrated unexpected behaviors including communicating with each other, bypassing monitoring systems, and attempting to access resources they were not supposed to use. He describes AI systems as “tendency learners” rather than simple instruction-followers, explaining how reward optimization can produce cheating, hacking, and attempts to evade oversight. The conversation also explores the possibility of AI manipulating human culture and psychology, effectively turning people into specialized “cells” serving a larger machine. Soares argues that the long-term outcomes range from humans becoming subordinate to AI systems to far more catastrophic scenarios, while emphasizing how little researchers understand about what is happening inside increasingly capable models.

title: Stanford CS153 Frontier Systems | Teaching AI to Touch Atoms
description:
For more information about Stanford's online Artificial Intelligence programs, visit: https://stanford.io/ai

Follow along with the course schedule and syllabus; visit: https://cs153.stanford.edu/

In this CS 153 Frontier Systems lecture, Periodic Labs cofounders Liam Ferriss and Dorje Chubak — veterans of OpenAI's post-training team and DeepMind's Genome project, respectively — walked students through their eleven-month-old mission to apply AI to the physical world, specifically using autonomous labs to accelerate the discovery of new materials including high-temperature superconductors. 

Operating out of a 40,000-square-foot Menlo Park facility where machine learning researchers work alongside physicists and chemists, their AI system (named Onnes, after the scientist who discovered superconductivity in 1908) runs a continuous loop of computational prediction, robotic synthesis, and experimental verification — closing the feedback cycle between digital intelligence and physical reality in a way no purely in-silico approach can. A key early lesson was abandoning their original plan of spending the first year purely computational: building smaller, semi-manual labs first allowed them to direct the research program and understand what to scale, faster. 

Dorje emphasized that the results of applying LLMs to actual atoms have exceeded even their own expectations, while Liam stressed that sample efficiency in reinforcement learning — not benchmark climbing — is the core technical frontier when physical experiments can't be arbitrarily scaled up the way digital rollouts can. They closed by pushing back on student anxiety about AGI displacing their careers, arguing that most scientific domains remain largely untouched by LLMs, that the bar to make meaningful AI-physical world progress is still surprisingly low, and that the history of civilization is essentially a materials story — making their work, in their view, among the highest-leverage bets anyone can make right now.

title: What Is Human in the Loop?
description:
When Should an AI Agent Ask for Permission? Amy and Sean from LangChain explain human in the loop, a design pattern where an agent pauses and waits for a human to approve before taking its next action. The best production agents use this deliberately: let the agent handle routine work, and only interrupt for high stakes actions. The best teams shipping the best agents are not going for full autonomy on day one, they build systems where humans and agents divide the work intelligently.

This is a clip from our full conversation where Amy and Sean answer the most commonly searched questions about AI agents, from the basics like what is an agent, what is RAG, and what is MCP, to harder questions like why agents hallucinate, how to evaluate them, and what LangChain actually does.

title: Build, Test, Deploy, Monitor: The Agent Development Lifecycle Explained
description:
Amy and Sean from LangChain break down the agent development lifecycle, the process agent engineers use to build and improve their agents. It comes down to four phases: build it in code with a framework like Deep Agents, test it with real inputs and expected outputs, deploy it into production, and monitor it with tracing and evals.

This is a clip from our full conversation where Amy and Sean answer the most commonly searched questions about AI agents, from the basics like what is an agent, what is RAG, and what is MCP, to harder questions like why agents hallucinate, how to evaluate them, and what LangChain actually does.

title: HTTP Channels for Managed Deep Agents
description:
Nathan Drezner, a product manager at LangChain, shows how to build a custom HTTP channel for a Managed Deep Agent so it can receive inbound requests from any service you don't control, like HubSpot, Salesforce, or a texting provider. He builds Reflex, an expense-reporting agent that receives receipt photos over iMessage through Photon, extracts the data, and stores it in durable memory backed by Context Hub. Along the way he covers writing verify and parse functions, managing thread IDs per user, sending replies with a post hook, checking the result in LangSmith, and when to reach for HTTP channels versus a custom UI on the LangGraph SDK.

description:

What exactly is an agent harness, and why is it the secret to fully autonomous coding? If your coding agents are hitting a wall, the problem might not be the model you are using, it might be the stack. In this episode of The Agent Factory, we break down how to stop relying on manual prompting and start building environments where AI can dynamically solve complex software engineering challenges.

First, we sit down with Ryan Lopopolo, the Google engineer who coined the term "agent harness". We will discuss why he hasn't manually written code since May, how to apply senior engineering principles to AI agents, and how agents are being deployed to operate Google Cloud. Then, Billy jumps into the code to demonstrate the difference between linear and closed-loop harnesses using the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Finally, Smitha reveals the three-layer stack you need to build high-performing agents today, featuring Gemini 3.8 Flash, Antigravity Boost, and the viral Google Skills GitHub repository.

Whether you are a developer trying to build your own agent loop, or a technical leader looking to scale AI autonomy across your infrastructure, you'll learn exactly how to configure the memory, tools, and guardrails necessary to make your agents reliable. You'll walk away with a clear understanding of when to use lightweight models for high-frequency loops, when to deploy orchestrators like Boost, and how to give your agents the precise domain knowledge they need to succeed.

title: Why Your AI Agent Fails in Production (And How to Catch It)
description:
Manual code  tweaking isn't a testing strategy. Here is how to actually evaluate AI agents for production. In this episode of AI Agent Clinic, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end evaluation pipeline in 60 minutes.

🔗 Repositories & Resources:
• Open-Source Agent-Eval Toolkit (GitHub):  https://g.dev/cloud/agent-eval 
• DocsHound Agent Code: https://g.dev/cloud/docshound 
• Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Docs: https://g.dev/cloud/agent-evaluation 

Most autonomous loops look great in local demos but fail silently in production. In this hands-on clinic, we compress weeks of testing setup into one hour by:
1. Mapping agent execution flow and inner workings using Antigravity
2. Standardizing multi-turn traces with OpenTelemetry & OpenInference (making your evals work across agentic frameworks like ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, or custom implementations)
3. Pairing custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluation rubrics and deterministic checkers for quality and performance assessment
4. Additionally, tracking  signals like: latency, token usage, and API cost
5. Ensuring zero vendor lock-in by building on open-source standards

Along the way, our automated scorecard catches a blind spot: a 33% documentation quality score that while eye-balling the results we initially missed.

title: What exactly is an Agent Harness?
description:
"Agent Harness" is the latest buzzword taking the AI world by storm, but what exactly does it mean?

In this video, Smitha Kolan and Luke Schlangen break down the anatomy of an AI Agent. You'll learn why an AI Agent is more than just a Large Language Model (LLM) and how the "Harness" provides the essential context and tools needed to solve complex, real-world problems.

What you’ll learn in this video:

-The Definition: Luke explains the simple formula: AI Agent = LLM + Agent Harness.
-Real-World Examples: See how Gemini Flash (the model) works with Google Anti-Gravity (the harness).
-Beyond Text-In, Text-Out: Why simple questions like "Why is the sky blue?" only need an LLM, but complex tasks like "Should I wear a raincoat?" require an Agent Harness to fetch real-time data.
-The Power of Context: How the harness wraps around the LLM to give it capabilities far beyond basic text generation.

Whether you're an AI enthusiast or a developer looking to build your first agent, this video will give you a clear understanding of the architecture behind modern AI.
